body_ar:
الحمد لله رب العالمين وصلى الله وسلم على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته.

أما بعد فإن من الحروف ما هو مختص ببعض الأحكام، فلا بد من العناية به للعناية بتلك الأحكام التي تختص به، وهذه الحروف هي الميم والنون واللام فهذه الحروف الثلاثة تخرج عن قواعد الحروف لبعض الاختصاصات التي تختص بها، فاحتيج لبيان أحكام تختص بها، وقد عقد المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى هذا الباب لبيان أحكام الميم ولبيان حكم النون المشددة فقال:

وأظهر الغنة من نون ومن** ميم إذا ما شددا....

هذه القاعدة تقتضي أن الميم والنون تزداد الغنة معهما في حال الادغام أي في حال التشديد، لأن كل واحد منهما في الأصل حرف أغن، فإذا تكرر ازداد نصيبه من الغنة، فلذلك لا بد من العناية بهما في حال التشديد ..
body_en:
Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. May God bless our Prophet Muhammad and grant him peace, and his family and his Companions and all who are guided by his guidance and follow his sunnah until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: among the letters are some that are singled out for certain rulings, and these must be attended to in order that those rulings peculiar to them may be attended to. These letters are the mīm, the nūn and the lām. These three letters depart from the rules of the letters, on account of certain particularities that belong to them, so there was a need to set out the rulings peculiar to them. The author, may God Most High have mercy on him, set out this chapter to explain the rulings of the mīm and to explain the ruling of the doubled nūn, and said:

*And make the nasalisation clear, from a nūn and from a mīm, when the two are doubled....*

This rule entails that with the mīm and the nūn the nasalisation is increased in the case of assimilation, that is, in the case of doubling — because each of the two is in origin a nasal letter, so that when it is repeated its share of nasalisation increases. For that reason the two must be attended to in the case of doubling ..

flags.arabic: وهذه الحروف هي الميم والنون واللام ... لبيان أحكام الميم ولبيان حكم النون المشددة
flags.context: the lām is named as one of the three letters with peculiar rulings but is not treated in the published text
options: translate as printed and note that the lām is not reached
treat the mention of the lām as an error
supply nothing and make no note
flags.note: The Sheikh names three letters — mīm, nūn and lām — and then says the author's chapter is set out for the rulings of the mīm and of the doubled nūn. The lām is not returned to before the excerpt ends. This may be because the chapter on the lām follows in the portion behind the download, or because the Sheikh is anticipating. Recorded so that a reviewer does not read the omission as a defect in the translation, and so that the lām is not silently dropped from the English.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The date shown by the CMS is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on the Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah, Ibn al-Jazari's versified primer on the rules of Qur'anic recitation. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 641–646 and the part numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the number in the title, not by id.

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text breaks off and the full material is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.
'Nasalisation' renders ghunnah, the nasal resonance carried by the letters mīm and nūn, and the central subject of the chapter.
'Doubling' renders tashdīd, the gemination marked by the shaddah, which the Sheikh here treats as the outcome of assimilation (idghām).

The single line of verse from al-Jazariyyah is rendered as prose in italics per the style guide, with the Arabic kept in the bilingual pane. The four dots after it are in the source and mark that the line is quoted only in part.
'In origin a nasal letter' renders ḥarf aghann — a letter that carries nasal resonance by its nature, before any rule of assimilation applies.
